subsubtopic: NORTHERN ONTARIO-PROGRAMS INTRODUCED BY FEDERAL GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the general election of 1980 returned 10 Liberal Members from northern Ontario-10. Yet, with all that representation under the previous Liberal administration, not once did one of those Liberal Members bring forward an economic program for their region.
1 am proud to say today that under the present Government the northern Ontario caucus of the P.C. Party delivered to the residents of northern Ontario.
We delivered an economic development program to the region.
We delivered $55 million in new federal money.
We delivered $15 million in loans and grants of up to a value of $60 million.
We delivered a secretariat, housed in our own back yard, to administer the program.
We delivered an advisory board made up of northern Ontarians. Mr. Speaker, the Government has delivered to northern Ontario.

subtopic: NEED FOR FORMULATION OF NATIONAL WATER POLICY
NEED FOR FORMULATION OF NATIONAL WATER POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in spring, 1984, the inquiry on federal water policy was launched to consult Canadians on a federal water strategy to meet our future needs. On September 30, 1985, the inquiry reported its recommendations to the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan). At that time the Minister stressed the urgency of

August 13, 1987
formulating a national water policy "to prevent the emerging crisis from happening".
The Minister has had the report for two years now and Canadians are wondering what he has done. The sense of urgency the Minister conveyed in September, 1985, seems to have evaporated like so much water on a hot summer's day. We urge the Minister to get going and start planning now to meet the water management challenges Canadians are facing now and will face in the years ahead. Canadians want to see the benefits of the 18 months of important consultations on water policy for Canada.

subtopic: PROPOSED TRANSPORTATION OF PLUTONIUM THROUGH CANADIAN AIRSPACE
PROPOSED TRANSPORTATION OF PLUTONIUM THROUGH CANADIAN AIRSPACE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the House the other day a question was asked of the Government about its position on the proposed flights of plutonium over the Canadian North. 1 found the government answer at that time to be very inadequate. All we received from the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Thacker) was the assurance that these flights could only occur with the full permission of the Canadian Government.
That is not the point, Mr. Speaker. The point is whether the Canadian Government is going to give permission for such flights, whether it will tolerate that type of danger to the northern environment.
I must wonder aloud just what is going on when the Government takes such a casual attitude toward that proposal. Is it because we have compromised ourselves with respect to radioactive substances in the North by the Government's proposal for nuclear submarines for Canada's North? Is it because the Government has entered into an agreement, through AECL, with the United States and Japan vis-a-vis the research going on at Lac du Bonnet into the disposal of high level radioactive waste? Is that why we have this silence, this incredibly relaxed attitude toward a very serious proposal? Or is it because of the general deference to all things nuclear to which the Conservatives have now become captive in the same way as the Liberals were before them?
All these things give one cause to wonder just what is going on. I think it is high time the Government paid some attention to this particular proposal.

Mr. Speaker, credit cards and interest rates do not seem to go together. For over two years my learned Conservative colleague, the Member for Scarborough West (Mr. Stackhouse), has been crusading to convince banks and department stores to act less greedily with their credit card interest rates.
The president of a Canadian shoe company told me that almost one-third of their net profits came from interest on overdue credit accounts. How silly. Whatever happened to good old cold cash and the rule of business ethics that, if you cannot afford to pay, you cannot afford to play?
We got ourselves into this trap by living plastic lives. We even buy our groceries now with a piece of plastic. However, banks and department stores are, in my opinion, charging excessively high interest rates on credit accounts. Persuasion has not prevailed. It is time to legislate. The Member for Scarborough West has my full support.

Mr. Speaker, last June 29 I rose in the House and urged the Minister of Environment (Mr. McMillan) to intervene with a view to settling a problem concerning log drives on the Saint-Maurice, the longest river used for such operations. This river flows through broad land expanses in the Mauricie region-from La Tuque to Trois-Rivieres-where logging operations are now one of the major sources of water pollution. This constitutes a very complex problem because, if ever consideration were given to banning log drives, the economic impact on our region would be catastrophic owing to the high cost of trucking logs over land.
Still, Mr. Speaker, I hardly think that letting the situation deteriorate will solve the problem. With this in mind, again I urge the Minister of Environment to convene all parties involved as soon as possible, namely Environment Canada, the paper companies concerned, other federal, provincial and municipal authorities, and spokesmen for the various users of the Saint-Maurice River.
August 13, 1987

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip's assistant; Deputy Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext:
Yesterday, Mr. Speaker, the leader of the socialist party flanked by 30-odd comrades, all excentrics with their own peculiarities, rose in this House to comment on the immigration measure in his capacity as party leader. The first part of his speech had to do with history and literature.
In the second part he simply echoes the message of pressure groups that are against the Government approach.
In the third part it becomes obvious that he is not living in 1987 because his leading references date back to 1914 and 1939.
He criticizes the Government position-which he has yet to read-and even wrongly states in his discourse that he did not get from the Minister a response to his personal quest for information.
In conclusion the socialist leader states that he wants to put an end to abuses and ban terrorism but he does not accept any of our means and, worse still for a party leader, he fails to suggest any alternative.
As he is wont, yesterday the socialist leader toyed with negativism, inaccuracies, demagogy and opportunism.

subtopic: WHITEWATER RAFTING FATALITIES-CALL FOR INTRODUCTION OF CONTROLS
WHITEWATER RAFTING FATALITIES-CALL FOR INTRODUCTION OF CONTROLS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, over the past year in my province of British Columbia we have seen 12 people die as a result of white water rafting accidents. Six of those tragic deaths have occurred in the last month alone.
1 have a letter from K. W. Stevenson, President of General Paint of Vancouver. He lost his daughter, Marie, aged 32, on the Elaho River north of Squamish. Mr. Stevenson says:
It is my sincere belief that government must introduce controls for ALL
rivers so that other families do not have to experience the grief that we have
felt.
I am sure all Members of the House will share in his grief over this tragedy.
I want to remind the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) that under the Canada Shipping Act the authority for regulating and maintaining safety standards on rivers remains with the federal Government and his Department.
I want to offer the co-operation of the New Democratic Party if the Government needs legislation to strengthen the
safety standards of rafting equipment and the qualifications of rafting guides. 1 have had the pleasure of rafting on the Fraser and Thompson Rivers, as perhaps you may have had, Mr. Speaker. It is great fun and it is a great tourist industry. However, we must make sure that these kinds of tragedies do not occur again.

Mr. Speaker, the majority of Canadians believe that legitimate refugees should be given safe haven in Canada. People want an immigration system that is fair and compassionate.
However, when the system is repeatedly abused, it is not unreasonable for the Government to tighten the refugee determination process, ensure visa compliance, and punish offenders.
I am very concerned that members of the New Democratic Party have not come clean on the issue of refugees. The Leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Broadbent) says the system should be tightened up, while many of his followers have delayed passage of immigration Bills, criticizing them as too severe.
If the NDP had not prevented earlier attempts to amend immigration laws, the recall of Parliament may not have been necessary.
The New Democratic Party should stop delaying new immigration laws. The Leader of the NDP should instruct a few of his loyal followers to act responsibly because Canadians deserve much better.

Mr. Speaker, in the late 1970s and early 1980s interest rates were high. The prime rate was over 20 per cent. Credit card companies, major retail stores and gas companies were charging around 25 per cent on unpaid accounts. When interest rates dropped substantially, the interest rates charged by these companies were not reduced.
It was only after questions in this House and after the finance committee brought down a report early this year criticizing these high interest rates, did the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Hockin) warn the charge card companies

August 13, 1987
that, if they did not cut their interest rates, Parliament would bring in legislation.
Finally, kicking and screaming, these companies brought down their interest rates somewhat a few months ago. Now, just four months after announcing a reduction in interest rates, they have begun to increase interest rates again. Their excuse is that interest rates have gone up somewhat.
1 call upon the Government to act now, not to wait for a Private Member's Bill which might, with luck, be dealt with a year from now. I call upon the Government to bring in the kind of legislation which will protect tens of thousands of Canadians from the greed of these giant companies.

subtopic: NORTHERN GARDENING PROGRAM SPONSORED BY MENNONITE CENTRAL COMMITTEE
NORTHERN GARDENING PROGRAM SPONSORED BY MENNONITE CENTRAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in many small communities in the North the price of produce is extremely high, yet the soil and climatic conditions are suitable for the growing of vegetables. A lacking ingredient, however, is knowledge and experience on the part of the inhabitants of how to cultivate gardens.
Recognizing this, the Mennonite Central Committee has, for the past several years, been sending experienced gardeners to the North to teach by example its people the art of horticulture. This is proving to be a successful program. The object of this statement is to thank both the Mennonite Central Committee and the individual participants for their continuing efforts on behalf of would-be northern gardeners.

Mr. Speaker, I stand in my place today to compliment the Government on the introduction of Bill C-84 which, in concert with Bill C-55, will stop the queue jumpers who are interfering with immigration to this country. These Bills will stop the unscrupulous tactics of a few people making money from the misfortunes of others with their boatloads of human contraband. That is not fair, nor is the open-door policy advocated by Members opposite.
With the passage of these Bills the Government will be able to proceed with plans to expand the family reunification program because, without immigration, Canada's growth rate will be negative. The Government wants to help bona fide refugees and immigrants enter this country. The hundreds of constituents who called my office to register their concern and
indignation demanded fairness. This is a trait which exemplifies Canadians and Canada to the rest of the world, and this Government is delivering.

Mr. Speaker, when you recalled the House to deal with Bill C-84 it was our intention at that time, of course, to co-operate with you and come back to Parliament. We have been debating this Bill now for two days.
It has been our intention, because it is very complicated and we have very many concerns which, of course, we have registered, to see amendments made to the Bill. Of course, the appropriate place to make those amendments is in a legislative committee. That is also the place where expert witnesses could be heard to help us improve the Bill. For that reason we have been anxious to have this matter referred to a legislative committee as soon as possible, ideally at the end of today, and that is still our wish.
We want to say we oppose the Bill. However, we want to do what we can to improve the Bill presently before the House and we can do that only by hearing expert witnesses in committee and by proposing amendments in committee.

Mr. Speaker, the recent western diversification initiative recognizes the need to develop and diversify the western economy to make it less vulnerable to international economic developments and fluctuating commodity prices.
A new agency, the Western Diversification Office, will be created under the leadership of the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. McKnight). The WDO, with offices in each of the four western provinces, will co-ordinate, support and encourage the creation of enterprises in the West and will administer a $1.2 billion Western Diversification Fund.
This new money will be used to promote western economic diversification by helping to support worth-while specific projects, by promoting the competitiveness of existing enterprise, and by facilitating the creation of new business.
August 13, 1987

The WDO will co-ordinate and communicate all federal programs and activities that contribute to the economic development and diversification of the West. The WDO and the $1.2 billion fund represent tangible proof of the Government's commitment to help improve the fortunes of western Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I just heard the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis) commenting on Bill C-84. He pointed out that although his party was opposed to the Bill, it wanted to see the Bill referred immediately to committee, so that witnesses could be heard.
I would like to say to the Hon. Member for Kamloops- Shuswap that his intellectual honesty leaves much to be desired. As a Member of this House, I have the right to express my views on Bill C-84, and I hope we will be given an opportunity to do so in this House. If his party is not prepared to come right out and say where it stands on this issue, preferring to hide in committee instead of speaking out in the House, it can go right ahead, but 1 want to express my opinion right here in the House. And I strenuously object to the position taken by the Hon. Member for the NDP on this matter.

subtopic: PATENT DRUG LEGISLATION-ATTITUDE OF UNITED STATES- GOVERNMENT POSITION

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: PATENT DRUG LEGISLATION-ATTITUDE OF UNITED STATES- GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister for International Trade. Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister. Last June 26 the Prime Minister said in this House that if there is the slightest doubt about the equality of women's rights in the Meech Lake Accord he will secure such rights at the next meeting with provincial premiers, with due speed.
Mr. Speaker, doubts have been raised and voiced by a number of constitutional experts. Now that these doubts have been expressed, can the Prime Minister unequivocally guarantee that he will do his utmost to obtain from his colleagues, the provincial premiers, an amendment giving women and minorities in Canada the absolute right to equality? My question is directed to the Prime Minister.

speakeroldname: Hon. Ray Hnatyshyn (Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: OPPORTUNITY TO INTRODUCE AMENDMENT GUARANTEEING EQUALITY FOR WOMEN AND MINORITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 appreciate the Hon. Member's question. 1 think it is important to understand that in response to a similar representation the other day I tried to set out that we felt, on the best legal advice we were able to get, that indeed the rights of minorities and the equality rights with respect to women in fact remain protected under the Charter in a substantive way.
If she does not want to believe me, possibly she will believe Dean William R. Leterman of Queen's University who speaks on behalf of 12 leading experts on federalism from five Canadian universities and today stated:
In our judgment, the distinct society clause does not reduce federal
legislative authority; nor does it significantly impair citizen rights under the
Charter or the ability of Canada to recognize the rights of its aboriginal
peoples and its varied ethnic communities.
These are top-notch national experts who have indicated their support of this Accord as an absolutely essential political act on the part of this Parliament in the legislation of our country.

Mr. Speaker, my question was directed to the Prime Minister because the Prime Minister told us that if there were any ambiguity he would guarantee that he would secure the rights of women and dispel any such ambiguity. All I want to ask in my supplementary question is whether the Prime Minister has changed his mind since last June 26 and whether he is playing the same game as the Minister of Justice when refusing to acknowledge the ambiguity in the Meech Lake Accord? Who will make a decision? The Government or the courts?

Mr. Speaker, in his remarks the Hon. Member referred to five million refugees in the world. I would say that is probably a bit low. From the figures 1 have heard, I would think it is something like 15 million. What I would like to suggest to the Hon. Member is that they are not all coming here. They will.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
speechtext:
There are several questions there, Mr. Speaker. The first comment the Hon. Member made was totally erroneous. I never said there were five million refugees in the world. 1 would hope the Hon. Member has read the legislation a little more carefully than he listened to my speech.
There are 12 million to 15 million known refugees in the world according to the United Nations Human Rights Commissioner. What I said was that under the Singh decision with respect to the protection under the Charter, there is a possibility of five billion people. Anyone around the world could land on our shores. Whether an individual tells the truth or lies, if he says he is a refugee he is entitled to protection under the Charter. Therefore, potentially every person in the world can come here and claim refugee status. That confirms the numbers I quoted.
The Hon. Member wants to know, I believe, how we are going to decide, and that is at the heart of this legislation and at the heart of this debate, and what the Opposition is talking about, the definition of a legitimate refugee. The implication in everything opposition Members are saying is that the church groups and other groups to whom they have been talking have a right to decide and conclude who is or who is not a legitimate
August 13, 1987

refugee. What we are saying is that is not right. Everyone has to be subjected to the laws and regulations of Canada in determining whether or not they are legitimate. Otherwise we have a very subjective system. We can never have a dependable definition of what is a refugee if we are not going to do it according to law.
If the groups working with refugees have the right to bring their claimants to the border and say, we have already decided these are refugees and do not have to be subjected to analysis under the law, then we have a lot of favouritism in the system which we cannot tolerate. I think the Hon. Member knows that.
Therefore, I say again that 1 would hope that when the Hon. Member speaks in this debate, as 1 suspect he will, he will do so with a clear understanding of the provisions of the Bill. With respect to proposed Section 95.1 in which he is interested, let me propose to him that it is virtually impossible to come to Canada without some kind of documentation unless it has been destroyed. If a person comes under a scheduled airline, some kind of passenger system, he must have documentation before he gets on the airplane. If he comes by a scheduled ship, he must have documentation. The only way he can come without documentation is either by destroying it or by coming to a port of entry along the Canada-U.S. Border illegally. We are not going to allow organizations, with their own subjective criteria, to decide on behalf of the Department of Immigration and the court system of Canada whether or not those people who land on our shores or arrive at a port of entry are legitimate refugees.

On debate, the Hon. Member for Laurier (Mr. Berger).

Mr. Speaker, I am astounded by the remarks of the Hon. Member. For him to actually suggest that 5 billion people might come to Canada-

. . . that is beyond understanding, beyond reason . . .
[ English]
It is no small wonder that we are debating legislation which carries with it such abuses of our international obligations and the Charter of Rights. Indeed, the Hon. Member even admitted that Bills C-84 and C-55 are designed to do an end run around the Supreme Court of Canada, and around its decision in the Singh case.
Canadians are a fair-minded people. We often have difficulty in establishing that which sets us apart from other

August 13, 1987
Immigration Act, 1976
peoples. Most Canadians would agree that we possess a sense of fairness. The key issue in this debate is the fairness of the process. If Canadians today are upset with our refugee determination process, it is because the abuses they see offend their sense of fairness.
The critical questions we must ask ourselves are the following. How do we make it fair to both refugees and to immigrants, recognizing that we are dealing with two very different needs? How can we be fair to Canadians who have relatives who want to immigrate to Canada? What can we do to discourage widespread abuse so that Canadians will not feel that our immigration procedures are being by-passed? Surely, it is possible to devise a system that meets these needs.
Indeed, the proposals for reform of the refugee determination system made by Rabbi Gunther Plaut, and largely adopted by an all-Party parliamentary committee which included members of the government Party, show us the way to do it. These proposals are based on the simple premise that we can do justice to refugees, and discourage abuse, by providing claimants with a full and fair hearing, and a decision in a relatively short period of time.
The current system invites abuse. It takes from two to five years from the date a claimant arrives in Canada to the date of the final decision. People or illegal immigrants who may be inclined to abuse or take advantage of the current system do so because they know they can stay. If a quick determination was made within four or five months of that person's arrival in Canada, it would remove abusers and allow refugees to begin to rebuild their lives quickly. In this manner, we would respond to the needs of refugees, and most abusers would not come. The cost would be prohibitive for an illegal immigrant to come here and be sent home shortly afterwards. By cutting down the time for a decision, abuse is eliminated. TThe confidence of Canadians in our system and laws would be restored.
The other half of the equation is the refugee. How can we be fair to refugees? Rabbi Plaut went to great lengths in outlining the manner in which to be fair to refugees. He insisted on the need for independence of the refugee board, and the right to counsel. He argued that while it is necessary to shorten the process to a minimum, a certain minimum period of time is required for refugee claimants to adequately prepare their cases; the need for procedural fairness should be obvious. Refugees have left their homes because of war and persecution. Their lives and liberty are at stake. Even refugee claimants who one might expect to be fairly articulate, such as lawyers, teachers, and union leaders, have been known to break down during refugee hearings; they have been unable to face the past, unable to talk about the experiences to which that they have been subjected. We must understand that refugee claimants are in a new country, probably they do not speak either English or French. Unquestionably, they are unfamiliar with our laws and procedures.
In his report, Rabbi Plaut considered and rejected various means of arbitrarily excluding certain groups of persons from
presenting their claims. The refugee determination system should be open to all claimants; that is, any person arriving in Canada and claiming to be a refugee ought to be given a hearing, and an opportunity to present his or her individual case and be judged on the merits of the claim. This corresponds to the sense of fairness of all Canadians.
Rather than allowing all refugee claimants access, the Government proposes to screen out claimants before they have had a full hearing on the merits, if they come from so-called third safe countries, or if they are unable to establish what the Government refers to as a credible basis for their claims within 72 hours of arrival in Canada.
Rabbi Plaut looked at these concepts and he rejected them. He rejected the idea of screening out those with what are known as "manifestly unfounded claims". He reviewed the practice in those countries that have tried to introduce such a practice only to find it to be unworkable, in other countries, some cases which were at first judged to be manifestly unfounded claims eventually were determined to be refugees by a higher authority.
However, the Government in its wisdom rejected his advice. Under the Government's legislation claimants from countries on a predetermined list established by Cabinet, which may have nothing to do with their personal circumstances, will not get a hearing. There will be no opportunity for them to refute the assumption established by Cabinet that the country to which the Government wants to return them is indeed safe. The inquiry will be limited to determining from where the person came. Members of the Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration have been warned about the dangers of such a practice. Representatives of the United Nations High Commission on Refugees in Canada told the committee the following in March of this year:
Pakistan may be safe for Afghans in general but not for Iranians-as for Afghans, you have to listen to the claim. There are different political and religious parties among the Afghans. Some of them have good relationships with the government and others do not . . . so even for Afghans who in general are very well treated in Pakistan, we would have to investigate the claim of the individual before saying this man is an Afghan and can be sent back to Pakistan.
Similarly, in the last week or two an Iranian was murdered by one of the Ayatollah's hit men in Europe. This is not the first time it has happened. Many former supporters of the late Shah have been murdered on the streets of Paris and London. Europe is clearly not safe for some Iranians. Some may be safe-people who are not notable members of the community or perhaps young people. However, clearly Europe is not safe for certain individual Iranians. They should not be arbitrarily excluded from our refugee determination process because Cabinet decides, in its imagination, that European countries are safe for Iranians. We must look at each individual case. We must allow people to present their claims and to be judged.
August 13, 1987

It is false for the Minister, it is false for the Parliamentary Secretary, and it is false for every member of the Conservative Party to say that no genuine refugee will be returned to a country where he or she may face persecution or death; this is just not so. The procedure the Government proposes provides no opportunity for the refugee to make his or her case.
Also it is false for the Minister to say that in all cases the refugee will be given the benefit of the doubt and that even when there is a shred of evidence supporting the claim, as the Minister has said on countless occasions, the claimant will be entitled to a fair hearing. This is just not so. It is not supported by the law before us today.

Instead of advocating giving refugees an honest and fair hearing, the Government proposals totally disregard the consensus flowing from consultations held by Rabbi Plaut and by the House standing committee, consultations to which the Canadian Bar, church authorities and non-government organizations were party. Instead of providing universal access to the system, Mr. Speaker, the Government is suggesting that applications be pre-screened on the basis of arbitrary criteria. Instead of allowing refugees to prepare adequately for a hearing where their life and freedom are at stake, the Government wants to force them through a hearing within 72 hours of their arrival in Canada. Instead of guaranteeing a refugee the right to a lawyer or counsel of his choice, this hasty process denies this basic right as guaranteed by our Charter of Rights. We must bear in mind the situation of refugees: not only is Canada a foreign country to them, but in most instances they do not know a soul here. More often than not they are advised by non-government organizations, refugee assistance agencies and church representatives. These organizations rely on volunteers and are forever strapped for financial resources. So how do you expect these organizations to intervene within 72 hours? Is there one individual who is prepared to say that refugees will be treated fairly and equitably under this system?

If fairness is the issue, there are further considerations. When Canadians travel abroad or participate in international meetings, we are often pleasantly surprised by the strong and considerable reputation of Canada. This reputation is founded on our contributions to the international community, going back to the days of Pearson, to our peacekeeping efforts, and to our record of aid to Third World countries.
The generosity of Canadians has also extended to refugees. In 1986 the Nansen Medal was awarded to the people of Canada by the United Nations. Who was Nansen? He was a Norwegian, an Arctic explorer, and oceanographer, best remembered for his work for the relief of suffering peoples. He was responsible for the repatriation from Russia of 500,000 prisoners of war from the German and Austro-Hungarian armies. In 1921 he succeeded in raising funds to bring relief to famine-stricken Russia. In 1922, at his initiative, an international agreement was signed in Geneva, introducing the
Immigration Act, 1976
identification card for displaced persons, known as the Nansen passport.
Think of the cruel irony. In 1986 Canadian people received a medal named after Nansen who gave displaced persons, persons without documentation, identification cards. In 1987 the Government wants to throw refugees without documents in jail.
The reputation of our country is also due to its nature. I have been impressed on visits abroad about the advantages of living in and coming from a bilingual country. There is hardly a world forum in which we do not participate. We are involved in the Commonwealth and La Francophonie. When I visited a refugee camp on the border of Thailand and Cambodia I was filled with pride on meeting Canadian volunteers, doctors, and nurses who acted as interpreters between Americans who spoke no French and Belgians or French who spoke no English. To me that is how Canadians can play a special role in the international community.
We are seen as a principled nation, a caring nation, and we ought to be concerned about the effect of this legislation on the international community and on how other countries treat refugees. We have to be concerned about the effect of this legislation on the UN Convention. The basic thrust of this legislation is that the Government does not want refugees to make claims in Canada. It wants to select refugees abroad, something which we do more out of our need for immigration than out of concern for the plight of refugees.
The Minister does not say so directly-

. . . The question was put to the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard) the other night when he was being interviewed on Le Point'. How do you expect refugees to come to Canada? He replied: Let them come any way they can.
But they want to deny them any way to come to Canada without first filing an application with our embassies abroad.

Line up abroad, that is what this Government is saying. That is why the Minister wants increased fines for transportation companies. 1 ask you, Mr. Speaker, what will happen if all countries tell refugees to line up abroad? What will happen to refugees fleeing for their lives if all they have is the right to wait in line and apply to immigrate from an embassy in a country where they face persecution? Should Canada not be leading the fight to preserve the United Nations Convention so that refugees can continue to have the ability to effect some salvation on their own, to move spontaneously to a safe haven without visas, without lining up at an embassy door or without proper documentation? That is the whole purpose of the United Nations Convention.

August 13, 1987
Immigration Act, 1976
Is it fair for Canada to lead the world in denying refugees this right?

speechtext: Are there questions or comments?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Elon. Member spoke at some length on the subject of screening. In that respect 1 have one question that I would like to put to him.
In 1980, the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy) was the Minister of Immigration. At that time there was a very famous case involving a gentleman by the name of Mr. Giuseppe Calamusa who had been convicted in Italy of three criminal offences. He came to Canada illegally in 1968. He was deported on five occasions and charged in Toronto with counterfeiting. He skipped bail in 1976, and in 1977 he was convicted and imprisoned. Sometime after 1980 he got into his car and drove to Winnipeg, turned up at the then Minister's office and asked for a ministerial permit. The Minister had a member of his staff drive this gentleman in a government car down to Emerson, Manitoba, where they did a loop around the immigration building and then presented him with a ministerial permit.
In view of the Hon. Member's interest in screening can he tell me whether the former Minister of Immigration, the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry, had prospective immigrants properly screened or was that his idea of screening people who should be admitted into Canada?

Mr. Speaker, I am only vaguely familiar with the facts of the case to which the Hon. Member refers. I recall the name, perhaps as a result of questions having been raised in the House. I would like to ask the Hon. Member what that has to do with the debate we are having here today? Was this person admitted into Canada as a refugee? Was he admitted as a landed immigrant under immigration procedures or under refugee procedures? Quite frankly, I do not know what the Hon. Member is talking about. I wonder if he does.

Mr. Speaker, I know that the Hon. Member for Laurier (Mr. Berger) has demonstrated his concern for Convention refugees by visiting with me refugee camps in Thailand and Malaysia. He has participated in the process of bringing refugees to Canada through the legitimate route laid down by the United Nations Convention. Does the Hon. Member feel that it is fair that illegal aliens should be able to jump the refugee process by coming directly to Canada? Does he not agree that the 12 million refugees in refugee camps around the world, Convention refugees as designated by the United Nations, who have been waiting for months and years and who perhaps will never be received, should have priority and that the system should be respected? Those 12 million people are equally concerned with this situation and do not like the line-jumping either. Does the Hon. Member not agree that they have a prior right and that we should try to preserve the system?

Mr. Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for his kind remarks. We ought to go on another trip again soon. It was very enjoyable, not because it was a joy-ride-it was not. On the contrary, it was hard work, but we were working for a good cause.
Does the Hon. Member not recognize that some of the people who have been accepted as refugees by making claims in Canada have been recognized as refugees? Are those people not legitimate? Is that not what we are trying to preserve? Is that not why we are so upset because of an arbitrary screening process that would possibly and inevitably rule out some of those people?
Does the Hon. Member not recognize that the concerns we have and the concerns experts have, including Rabbi Plaut, are legitimate? Does he think that the only wisdom is on the government side?

Mr. Speaker, I would like to remind the Hon. Member that it would appear, although it has not been proven yet, that perhaps some of these refugees tried to come through a third country. They, for example, bypassed Germany, thus bypassing all the refugees in the camps there. They could have gone there and got into the process in that way. Surely the Hon. Member understands that there must be a system, a system which does not allow bypassing of third countries. Surely he understands that we cannot allow racketeers or privateers to abuse that system any more than the pirates off Thailand can be allowed to continue their piracy. Until we can establish a better system, we must maintain control, not only in the interest of Canada but in the interest of the 12 million refugees who want to come here or to other countries. Linejumping cannot be allowed to continue if we are to be just and fair.

Mr. Speaker, 1 would ask the Hon. Member to think through his argument. He said that some of these people have come to Canada through a third country. Sure, they come through a third country. We do not have any refugee-producing states on our borders. If people had to come directly from a refugee-producing state in order to claim refugee status no one would be able to make a claim in Canada. The whole purpose of the Convention is to allow people to make claims, to move spontaneously on their own.
As long as human beings have a breath of life in them, as long as they have a desire to survive, they will find ways around the bureaucratic systems established by Governments. They will find ways to save their lives. They will find ways of not lingering in refugee camps.
I would like the Hon. Member to reflect on the fact that in the 1920s and the 1930s, there was a Canadian immigration regulation which said that one could not immigrate to Canada if one could not come here by continuous journey.

Same rule for the same purpose.
August 13, 1987

It is the same rule that we are talking about today, a rule which was discredited in those times.
I would ask the Hon. Member to read a speech I made some months ago in which I quoted a predecessor of mine, Sam Jacobs, who used to say that if Jesus of Nazareth had to come to Canada under that kind of system, he would have been refused entry because he could not have come here by continuous journey. There were a few other factors which would have been in his way as well.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jake Epp (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, thank you for giving me some time today to address Bill C-84. I would like to put a few of my views on the record, views which will hopefully help this debate. I know that this debate has been fairly intensive on both sides of the House, but I think there are some issues on which we agree and I think we should take a look at how we can go from there.
From 1973 to 1979, I had responsibilities as immigration critic while we were in opposition. At that time, the then Government presented a Green Paper on immigration and we travelled the country to get the views of Canadians, many of which were similar to the views that are being expressed in this debate. Legislation was then introduced and this legislation still primarily governs immigration in Canada today.
At that time, though there were differences of opinions on specific points, there was also a lot of agreement on the immigration legislation. The principles on which it was based at that time still exist today and those principles must be repeated. First, Canada needs more immigrants. 1 believe that that is not a point that is at issue in the House of Commons.
Let me put on my hat as Minister of National Health and Welfare. Demographic studies and projections for Canada are being conducted in my Department on behalf of the Government and are made public. From those studies, it becomes evident very quickly to any objective observer that Canada has benefited greatly from immigration. I do not think we could describe Canada without describing the immigration flow as that is the nature of Canada.
From a demographic point of view, we do need more immigration. Comparing the aging population in Canada to the fertility rates of Canadian women of child-bearing age, it becomes clear very quickly that we do need more immigration, and I believe that on that point we do agree.
Immigration Act, 1976
Second, I think we all agree that Canada has accepted refugees, is presently accepting refugees, and should and will accept refugees in the future. I believe it is important to keep that in mind. Today's debate, despite its intensity, is not about whether or not Canada should accept refugees. The question is, however, how people should be accepted as refugees.
Third, each country in the world, no matter how generous it is in receiving immigrants, has taken upon itself as part of its sovereignty both the right and the responsibility to put both legal and regulatory conditions on how people enter the country. That is part and parcel of the sovereignty of a country. I believe that some Canadians feel today that Canada's ability to control the manner in which people enter the country has been seriously jeopardized, and that is a fundamental principle underlying the actions of the Government.
I would hope that there is no disagreement among all sides of the House on those three points. If that is the case, then let us look at the record.
Quite frankly, I was more saddened than shocked by some of the words used by the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy) to describe my friend and colleague, the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard). To say that someone is barbaric is something that surely should not flow from the lips of a Member of Parliament when describing another Member, whether inside the House or out.
I do not think I am giving away any cabinet confidences when 1 say that I know that the Minister of Employment and Immigration has always said that we need more immigrants. To use words to describe him like those used by the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry is totally unacceptable.
On page 8005 of yesterday's Hansard, the Hon. Member alludes to the fact that the Minister could possibly be racist because he wants to accept immigrants on the following basis:
They want to decide whether it is the colour of their skin or their hair or
their religion which determines whether they are bona fide refugees.
I believe that most objective observers would say that when using those kinds of words, one is ascribing to a person racial overtones. I do not think that has a place either in this House or in this debate. I feel more sorrow than anything else when 1 hear that kind of a description of my hon. friend and colleague, the Minister of Employment and Immigration.
If those principles to which I have referred apply, it is very interesting to note what has happened to immigration in the last 10 years. Combining refugee and designated classes, in 1978, Canada landed 913 people. The law changed at that time, so that has to be taken into consideration.
I am not trying to be partisan because the pattern continued after our defeat in 1980, but in 1979, the Government said that it would take more boat people from Indochina and we asked church groups, NGOs and others to co-operate. They

August 13, 1987
Immigration Act, 1976
co-operated beyond any of our expectations in the best Canadian tradition. That year, we landed 27,528 refugees.
In 1980, as that program came into full bloom, that figure was 40,348. Then in 1981, the figure went down to 14,979. Who was the Minister then? It was the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy). The next year it was 16,925. It then dropped to 13,967 in 1983. In 1984, it started going up, to 15,342. In 1985, it went up to 16,760. In 1986, 17,145. Up to the end of June of this year we are at 12,168. Assuming roughly the same amount in the second six months, the number could be well over 20,000 for the year.
The point I am making is that the Opposition says this Government is against refugees, and that is absolutely wrong. The numbers point the other way. I ask the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry and his colleagues why fulminate against this Government today when their Government had a rate lower than either the Government of 1979-80 or this Government?
We are talking about the legislation you are introducing today, you jerk.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: At least I finally have his attention. He does not want to face the truth.
Talk about this Bill.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
I will talk about this legislation. The Minister said that we will continue not only the present level of immigration, he said on second reading that he was willing to signal to the House when he is obligated under the legislation, an amendment I moved at that time, to come in with higher targets. Surely we have to go with the evidence rather than the rhetoric or emotions such as demonstrated by the Hon. Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia).
The second point I would like to make is that there has been a change. That change flowed from the Singh case. This has to be understood. To every country in the world that receives immigrants, including Switzerland, Sweden, the U.S. and the U.K., when a person sets foot on its territory that person is deemed not to be in the country for the purpose of exercising all legislative rights until that person's status had been regularized. That was a convenient legal way of being able to determine what that person's status was. It gave the country the power of maintaining its regulations and its sovereignty. In Canada the Singh case reversed that. To my understanding, this is the only country in the world faced with that situation. That interim period is no longer considered valid under our Charter of Rights. Therefore, if a person comes into this country, legally or illegally, from the moment he or she touches Canadian soil they are covered by the Charter and the need for an oral hearing.
The point is that one can see very quickly why our immigration laws have to be changed. Not to reduce the number of
refugees who are coming here legally but so that people cannot thwart either the will of Parliament or the fair judgment of Canadians.
What about the UN Convention?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
The Hon. Member refers to the UN Convention. I have it here before me because that is the next point I wanted to make.
The Opposition says that what we are doing is a violation of the UN Convention. That is not what the UN Commissioner for Refugees says at all. However, if that is the case, is Switzerland outside the convention? Are Sweden and Norway outside the convention? To ask the question is to answer it. It is simply not true. It might be a point of debate but it is not true. If one looks at the comments of the UN Commissioner relative to Bill C-55, a Bill which is not before us but which is tandem to Bill C-84, you will find that he would like to recommend some changes to Bill C-55 to "have as good a model of refugee acceptance as possible". Obviously he is trying to work towards the ideal model. He indicates very clearly, "The UNHCR does not suggest that any aspects of the proposed system are contrary to the convention".
This Government will maintain its international obligations. We are not in contravention of those obligations. This Government will maintain the historic traditions of Canada with respect to immigrants and refugees. However, we cannot violate a system so that anyone in the world can take it upon himself or herself to come to Canada and have rights which they do not have anywhere else in determining the manner in which they stay or how long they stay. That is fair and that is just.
Let us come now to the matter of destroyed documentation. It is interesting to note that a number of people who have come here to Canada to claim refugee status, before they were able to get on a conveyance to Canada, in most cases airlines, they had to have proper documentation. If they did not, I suggest in many cases the airline would not have accepted them as passengers. Therefore, one has to ask: Why destroy the documents? Is the Opposition saying that because someone destroys their travel documents they should have some right of access to the system before those who are in refugee camps? Is that the argument they want to put forward?
I suggest that the reason these people are destroying documents is that a number of them have status-
They are fraudulent documents.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
I will get to that, too. We have had indications just recently of people who have come here and had status in Denmark. They chose to get on an aircraft to Canada and before landing they destroyed their documents in order that it would not be known they had status in Denmark. That is the kind of thing we are dealing with. Yes, there are fraudulent documents, but surely it is incumbent upon the Government of any country to check first on whether they are
August 13, 1987

fraudulent. Surely Canadians expect nothing less from their Government.
There are those who will argue that we should have universal access. They do not like to put it quite that way but that is the result of their argument.
We put it exactly that way.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: So you are in favour of universal access?
Yes, I am!

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: All right, let us look at that. The Hon. Member for Laurier (Mr. Berger) says exactly what he is in favour of. He is saying to Canadians, and they have to understand this, that everyone who decides to come to Canada and claim refugee status should have access.
Refugees.
Five billion people.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
If that is his argument, that is totally ludicrous. No Government of any country accepts that kind of principle. We hear, for example, about Sweden. Sweden is used as the ideal model. Sweden takes approximately 1,000 refugees a year. I have given you the numbers, Mr. Speaker, of refugees that Canada has taken and that the Minister says we will continue to take. It is interesting to note that when a person claims refugee status in Sweden the first government official he or she comes in contact with is a member of the state police.
1 think it is time that Canadians knew the facts and were not simply drawn to an emotional argument that Canada is the only country in the world which is being restrictive. In fact, how often do we hear that the United States is not a safe third country? The fact is that the United States has taken more refugees than any other country and Canada has taken the next highest number.
No it didn't.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: I am talking about refugees that have refugee status. We have U.N. obligations and humanitarian obligations, Mr. Speaker. We are saying very clearly that this legislation is needed to maintain those principles which have been part of Canada's traditions.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister was just referring to universal access as though people who are in favour of it had some kind of disease. I am in favour of universal access and I am proud of it. Rabbi Plaut is in favour of universal access as well. On page 91 of his report he says:
A guiding principle of refugee determination is that of access to the process.
It must be available to all refugees to ensure that we act according to the
principle of non-refoulement-
Immigration Act, 1976
-which is the most important and really the only obligation under the U.N. Convention.
Rabbi Plaut deals with the question of manifestly unfounded claims and the pre-screening process which the Government proposes to introduce. I would like to read to the Minister what he says about that. He quotes Professor Madsen and says:
-the noted scholar in the field, has observed that unstated administrative decisions of collective inadmissibility have endangered the refugee process in many countries.
The Minister was talking about practices in other countries. Does he not think that Canada has a responsibility to ensure that we preserve the system that was established in 1951? Does he not think that Canada has a special obligation? He talked about 18,000 people last year. He knows very well that that 18,000 included Portuguese and Turks and that the Government waited months before imposing visas on those countries. Why does he believe it is so necessary to impose artificial and unjustified screens on our refugee determination process?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Member and I disagree on a number of points. We have already stated our varying points on universal access. I do not believe that universal access works. No other refugee system has universal access. I have pointed out very clearly that the signal which the judgment on the Singh case sent to the world was that Canada's immigration laws worked.
The Member referred to 1951, and I think we must also refer to 1978. However, there were changing circumstances, both with the Charter and with the Singh case in 1985. I do not believe that universal access is the manner through which Canada should take the number of refugees which we have said we will. It is not in the Canadian interest to be the only country with universal access. We cannot send the signal to the rest of the world that that is the manner in which our system will work.
The Member said that we have a backlog. He knows that there was a backlog before the Government came into office, albeit not as large as it is today. The Minister has said that we need more resources, and I think that is absolutely correct, although I think those resources could have been in place earlier. However, since the signals from the Singh case became known worldwide the flow of refugee claimants has increased to the numbers that we have today.
Canada is not out of step. We are leading in terms of refugee determination and in terms of the hearings. The Member cannot give me examples of any country which accepts more refugees and has a more open policy than Canada would have with this legislation.

Mr. Speaker, one must judge a speech on the basis of whether it is credible and whether the speaker uses the facts and information in his hands in a proper and honest way. The statements just made by the Minister of National Health

August 13, 1987
Adjournment Debate
and Welfare (Mr. Epp) have totally and completely undermined his case. He has obviously attempted to use inaccurate and false figures which do not describe the conditions.
For example, he indicated that in 1984, the last year in which there was a Liberal Government dealing with refugees, there were only 15,342 refugees. I refer the Minister to the annual report tabled by the Department of Employment and Immigration which indicates that over 20,000 were in fact accepted. With regard to 1982, the Minister said there were something like 14,000 or 15,000. In fact, there were 22,000. He said that in 1983 there were 13,967. In fact, there were 17,000.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare, using the reports tabled by the Department itself, is using false and misleading figures. 1 think it is important that the record be corrected and that the Minister read the reports which were tabled by his own Department before he makes such allegations in the House. At least we could expect proper reading of the information and data as it exists, not as it is fabricated and manufactured.
I think the Minister of National Health and Welfare gave the game away when he said that he does not believe in universal access. He is in fact denying virtually every agreement we have signed internationally under the United Nations Covenant. Article 14 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights indicates that "everyone has the right to seek and to enjoy, in other countries, asylum from persecution". Everyone has the right to seek that in other countries.
The United Nations Declaration on Territorial Asylum, in Article 3(1), says that everyone has the right to the principle of non-rejection. Resolution (67)14 on Asylum to Persons in Danger of Persecution adopted by the Committee of Ministers of the Council of Europe, says the same. The OAU has the same provision.
What is perhaps most interesting is that the executive committee of the United Nations Commission on Refugees, on which a senior official of Canada sits, passed an executive order which specifically directs itself to the inequities of applying to transportation companies the responsibility of screening refugee applicants. In so doing, it says that it runs counter to the United Nations Convention and that we are the first country in that Convention to adopt that kind of practice. We are a member of the executive committee so they cannot plead ignorance. The executive committee went on to say:
The obligation to examine the claims of asylum-seekers cannot be delegated by States to private companies such as transport carriers. The Executive Committee of the High Commissioner's Programme has recommended in this regard that the determination of refugee status requires appropriate procedural guarantees including a complete personal interview by a fully-qualified official and. whenever possible, by an official of the authority competent to determine refugee status.
Does he mean to say that we are turning over to an airline attendant that responsibility which we, as a member of the executive committee, were adopting in this kind of resolution?
Once again, as we said in earlier remarks, the Government knows better. It has received contrary advice and now it is attempting to defend something that is totally indefensible. In the meantime, it is using false facts and figures to do it.
