The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Bouchard that Bill C-84, an Act to amend the Immigration Act, 1976 and the Criminal Code in consequence thereof, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.

Mr. Speaker, there are times in the history of a nation when the true character of that nation is tested. Those times are particularly times of fear and uncertainty.
When we look back to the history of our country, we can examine the response of Canada as a nation on those occasions. I think of the time in the 1940s, during World War II, when Canadians of Japanese origin were alleged to be threats to the security of Canada and, under the provisions of the War Measures Act, those Canadians were wrenched from their land, their homes and interned. That injustice has still not been remedied today.
I think as well back to 1970 when again it was alleged that there was a threat to the security of Canada sufficient to invoke the provisions of the War Measures Act once again, this time in peacetime. Over 200 Canadians were arrested in the middle of the night, never charged, and we recognize now that that was a serious abuse of the law.
They were threats to the security of our nation, yet now we see clearly that these events were in fact shameful blots on our history. They were based upon perceived threats which did not in fact exist in reality.
The opinion polls showed very clearly that 80 per cent or 90 per cent of Canadians supported the internment of Canadians of Japanese origin, supported the proclamation of the War Measures Act. Yet today, surely we as Canadians recognize that that was wrong.
I am proud that my Party and its predecessor, the CCF, was prepared to stand up in the face of that public opinion and recognize that this was wrong.
Once again, today, we see a Government which is prepared to take advantage of an atmosphere of fear, yes, and of uncertainty, to bring forward legislation that history will
Immigration Act, 1976
similarly condemn and that we in the NDP say is profoundly dangerous and constitutes an assault on the basic rights and freedoms set out in the Charter of Rights, in international conventions, and under international law. It is legislation that, in effect, constitutes a War Measures Act in the refugees area.
Once again, we have this abuse of the most basic and fundamental rights and liberties of the people on Canadian territory.
As a Member of Parliament from British Columbia, I recognize very clearly the concern that is felt by people in the face of what they perceive as injustice and as unfairness. As a Member of Parliament from British Columbia, and as the representative of the people of Burnaby, I want to make it very clear that my constituents-and I know that those of my colleagues feel the same-are concerned and angry about what they rightly perceive to be abuses of Canada's refugee determination system.
I have received hundreds of letters and telephone calls from my constituents. I have spoken personally with many of them. There are two or three basic themes which have emerged in the course of those conversations and in many letters and telephone calls. First, there is a deep sense of anger at what is perceived to be queue-jumping. People who have waited for members of their families to join them, in some cases for months or years, feel a sense of anger and injustice when others try to short circuit that process by filing phoney refugee claims. I think of the Turks, the Brazilians and the Portuguese who abused our system by claiming to be Jehovah Witnesses and being persecuted. Quite understandably, those who have been attempting to play by the rules are deeply offended when they see others who would abuse that system.
Second, my constituents, and 1 am sure most Canadians, are angered when they see others who would profit from and exploit those who are seeking to enter Canada, in some cases seeking to enter Canada illegally. Clearly, strong and effective legislation is needed to ensure that we respond to that kind of profiteering and exploitation of human misery.
Finally, the concern that I have heard, particularly from members of visible minorities, is one about a backlash. Yesterday, I even spoke with a young Canadian of Sikh origin from South Burnaby. He said that he has to work doubly hard now to have people accept him and his family. He was speaking of himself and his family and a backlash that has occurred against visible minorities in this country. There is a very large Sikh community in the Lower Mainland of British Columbia. I see the Hon. Member from Mississauga here. I know there is a large Sikh community in his area as well. The Sikh community in Canada is an overwhelmingly law-abiding, decent and upstanding community. Yet because of the actions of a very small minority there has been a backlash, and there has certainly been a backlash as a result of other recent events.

August 13, 1987
Immigration Act, 1976
Another young recent immigrant to Canada talked to me. He is from Vancouver. A few days previously he had read in the newspaper and seen on television a story about three people seeking refugee status. They were members of a wrestling team from Bulgaria. He asked me why it is that there seems to be a double standard, a sense of hypocrisy. The same Canadians who voiced their concerns-and I am not speaking here of all of them but certainly of some of them-about abuses in one area are silent when it comes to refugees whose skin happens to be of a different colour. These are the concerns which have been expressed about queue jumping, profiteering and about the effects of a backlash. These concerns have been expressed by the people of Burnaby, and I think they are felt generally by many Canadians.
The question we must surely ask ourselves is, has the Tory Government genuinely responded to these concerns in a sensitive way, or has it instead used these concerns as an excuse to bring in legislation which is dangerous, in breach of our international obligations, in breach of the provisions of the Immigration Act itself, which violates the fundamental guarantees set out in the Charter of Rights and Freedoms and that which ultimately condemn people fleeing persecution to certain torture or death? I suggest that it is the latter.
Let us examine whether the Government has really succeeded in dealing with genuine concerns, that is that there not be an abuse of the system and there not be profiteering. One part of this legislation would make it a criminal act for church groups, Amnesty International or for individual Canadians to assist refugees attempting to flee from repressive regimes to enter Canada, refugees who do not have travel documents. How can it possibly be suggested that a church group, be it the Mennonite Church or any other group, which seeks to assist a family fleeing from the murderous regime in El Salvador who arrives on Canada's border without a travel document, will be subject to prosecution, to fines and to jail? Clearly this is totally unacceptable.
Twenty-five percent of the refugees who seek to enter Canada in fact are not in possession of documents, and that is not surprising in many cases. This Bill would permit the detention of these individuals for up to 28 days in jail. Surely that is a step backward. It would permit the wire tap and the seizing of cars, for example, of those church groups and other volunteer organization which assist individuals who are fleeing from oppression in other parts of the world.
We certainly would agree with legislation that would attack those who would profit from the entry into Canada of illegal immigrants or refugees, those who would attempt to take advantage of clandestine entry in order to make money. That we would support. However, we reject an approach which would be subject to criminal sanction those who would assist genuine refugees.
Clause 8 of the legislation would allow the Government to turn away a ship which lands on Canada's shore without
affording to those on board that ship a basic hearing to ensure that indeed they are not genuine refugees. That provision of this legislation is clearly in breach of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms as interpreted by the Supreme Court of Canada. The Supreme Court of Canada in the Singh decision made it clear that the Charter of Rights requires an oral hearing for all who claim refugee status in Canada. This Bill would deny that. Who would make the decision to turn the ship away, a Coast Guard official? That would be totally unacceptable to this Party.
We say again that we must examine Canada's history and recognize clearly that in 1914 with the Komagata Maru and in 1939 with the St. Louis, we condemned refugees to death. We must never again adopt legislation which would allow for that possibility.
Another area of concern is the provision with respect to security. As this legislation stands, the Bill would allow genuine refugees to be denied access to the refugee process if a certificate is filed suggesting they may be a threat to the security of Canada. Who provides that information? The information is provided by CSIS. The Security Intelligence Review Committee has said in it most recent report that CSIS does not understand that the foreign policy objectives of our allies and of other countries are not necessarily Canada's foreign policy objectives, which could condemn many refugees to torture or death.
Those are some concerns with respect to the legislation. The Bill flies in the face of our existing commitments under international law and it flies in the face of Section 3 of the Immigration Act itself which requires Canada to fulfil our international legal obligations with respect to refugees and to uphold its humanitarian tradition with respect to the displaced and the persecuted.
In closing, 1 want to point out that there is another route. The present law obviously is not satisfactory. It has led to abuses and to lengthy delays in the refugee determination process. People have taken advantage of those delays. However, in 1985, the Parliamentary Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration came up with a unanimous report urging the Government to adopt a system which would ensure that there are in fact hearings and that our obligations under international law and the Charter would be respected. Not only that committee, but the Hon. Member for La Prairie (Mr. Jourdenais), from whom we will be hearing in just a moment, stated that the refugee legislation tabled by the Government, Bill C-55, would make it almost impossible for genuine refugees to make a claim. The Hon. Member said the procedure set out to adjudicate claims to refugee status in the Bill is fundamentally flawed. We will have an opportunity to hear directly from that Hon. Member.
In conclusion, I wish to say that this Bill is wrong. The Government is pandering to the deepest fears and insecurities
August 13, 1987

of Canadians. It is offering a false and dangerous solution. It is a shameful trampling on the basic rights and freedoms of genuine refugees who seek to claim refugee status. It is an implementation of that policy which was eloquently described by Irving Abella in his book with respect to the closing of the doors on immigrants and Jewish refugees: "None was too many". If this Bill is adopted, quite clearly we will threaten the lives of people who are fleeing from tyranny and oppression.
We in the House, and we in the New Democratic Party, will not accept that fundamental denial of Canada's obligations and traditions under international law.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: On debate, the Hon. Member for La Prairie (Mr. Jourdenais).

Mr. Speaker, this is a very important day for me and for all Canadian men and women. A great many Members in this House and a number of people outside are impatiently waiting for my reaction to Bill C-84. Today and tomorrow, I as Member for La Prairie, like Lot, will open my door to strangers, these men and women, these children and these old people who have been seeking refuge here. Let us protect them.
Over the past few hours I read and re-read Bill C-84. I discussed the issue with the highest-ranking civil and religious authorities of this country. Yes, last evening I had a very long meeting with the Right Hon. the Prime Minister and leader of my Party. I had lengthy discussions with spokesmen for immigrant and refugee service organizations. I also spoke with Canadian Bar representatives. I also had telephone conversations with representatives of international organizations, including the United Nations. And I took refuge in the Book of Ecclesiastes, a work of wisdom written more than 3,000 years ago. Then I got to work, I began observing all acts of oppression committed under the sun, everywhere oppressed people crying and nobody to comfort them. Harshly treated by their tyrants, there is no one to help them. I noticed that the labour of man and his every effort to succeed are motivated by the jealousy he feels towards his fellow man. Again this is "vanity and vexation of spirit", chapter 4, verses 6, 8.
In recent months, Mr. Speaker, the media have often highlighted how cumbersome and time-consuming the refugee status determination process is in Canada as it applies to people seeking protection against persecution. Were we to complete every prescribed stage, such determination might take from two to five years. And delays breed abuses, Mr. Speaker, because status applicants have precious little to lose by working five years in Canada as they wait, perhaps to be deported some day. Very obviously a reform is urgent. All refugee organizations have been asking for one for a number of years. Mr. Speaker, the Government has released a whole series of studies and reports on this issue. Many private agencies have also submitted briefs and recommendations.
Immigration Act, 1976
Joint consultations have been held, and the House of Commons Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration which I am proud to chair has also made recommendations in this field.
Today, years after problems have been identified and solutions advocated, Parliament is about to come up with concrete measures. Unfortunately, this desire for action stems from a series of irregular incidents rather than from humanitarian motives, or quite simply because of the need to update an old statute.
In 1987 the Government introduced Bill C-55, an Act to amend the Immigration Act.
The changes in the refugee determination process which are proposed in this bill are such that it would be practically impossible for a great number of legitimate refugees to apply for refugee status. Not to mention that the provisions of the bill probably go against the United Nations Convention on the Status of Refugees, which Canada has signed and ratified, as well as against our own Charter of rights and freedoms. In July, 1987, after 174 Sikhs claiming refugee status had landed on the coast of Nova Scotia, the Government announced that it would tighten its legislation.
There are, I am sure, other rational and appropriate solutions to this problem, solutions that would not have us break an international agreement on refugees and that could not be challenged in court on the basis of the Canadian Charter of rights and freedoms.
Years of reports, debate and recommendations have brought to light such principles and methods as would allow Canada to determine refugee status in a swift and equitable way in response to applications of would be refugees.

Short-term problems stem from long-term inadequacies of policy. Canadian immigration policy is tighter now, on a proportionate basis, than it has been at any time in our history, except during the Depression years. If our over-all immigration levels are low, our refugee numbers are laughable. For example, last year 1,000 places were allotted to the continent of Africa. The result of this overly restrictive stance has been to create a good many illegal immigrants and, second, to establish a market for smugglers and con artists. That is why we are here today. It piles yet more people into the hopper of an already heavily backlogged system. It forces periodic amnesty to be declared to clear the backlog, thereby encouraging still more desperate attempts to jump the queue, which starts the cycle all over again.
The best way to put the smugglers out of business is to dry up the demand for their services. The best way to stop the queue jumping is to shorten the queue. In short, if we want more orderly borders, we need more liberal borders.
Hear, hear!

I did not use the word "liberal" as a Party, I used it as a liberal policy to do it.

August 13, 1987
Immigration Act, 1976
Establishing a quicker, clearer process at the same time would also help to cut the backlog and hence reduce the incentive to overload the system in hopes of an amnesty. Instead, the Government intends to tighten the admission of refugees via Bill C-55, which will guarantee that the process remain arbitrary, confusing, and endless.
There may be a case for this type of rough, frontier justice if immigration were harmful to the country. We need look no further for evidence to the contrary than ourselves, our parents, and their parents. We may also look at the success of the Tamils in the year since their arrival. Yet, the same myths that immigration raises unemployment, depresses wages, and others such myths that are less respectable still persist today. Those were the myths that were used to try to keep out our grandfathers.
There is no natural population level for Canada. If there were, it is remarkable that it should so often be assumed to be the present level. Moreover, there are economic benefits to having more people, especially more immigrants. Larger populations mean economies of scale. Regular infusion of skills, resourcefulness, and entrepreneurial drive that immigrants typically bring to Canadians can only be healthy. Unless immigration is markedly increased, a declining fertility rate will mean an aging, dwindling population in years to come. Our immigration problem is too few people, not too many.
No one knows what the correct level of immigration is, or what it should be. It is a safe bet that it is very much higher than it is at present. To bring us up to our historical average as a proportion of population would mean an intake of 275,000 people per year. However, if we are to welcome greater numbers of immigrants in years to come, then the Government must begin now to prepare the way. It must educate the public on the real value of immigrants who arrive on our shores and stop racism. They do us a favour by coming to Canada; it is not the other way around. It must appeal to our highest selves, not appease the instinctive fear of a stranger at our door.
The recent increase in the movement of asylum seekers from the Third World into the countries of western Europe and North America has become a serious preoccupation of Governments in those regions. These movements, when seen in the context of a parallel migratory flow from the poorer nations toward these same countries, have given rise to concern for Governments and populations alike.
Many affected countries have reacted with a variety of legal and administrative measures aimed at stemming the flow. These measures include the introduction of visa requirements for nationals of particular countries and the imposition of sanctions on transport carriers for transporting illegal immigrants from these or any other country.
The United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees is concerned that measures taken to maintain such movements
affect asylum seekers who are in need of protection. Such concern may not arise if the measures were to be limited to countries which do not normally produce refugees. However, when they are applied to persons leaving countries which produce refugees, they may have very serious consequences for the protection of refugees.
In this context it should be noted that persons wishing to leave their country of origin in search of asylum elsewhere may often not be able to depart in a regular manner and in possession of full documentation. Similar considerations often apply to persons who, for reasons of personal security, are compelled to leave another country where they originally had been considered to have found protection.
With regard to sanctions against transport companies carrying aliens without proper documentation, they give rise to serious concern that no distinction is made between aliens in general and asylum seekers in search of international protection.
Hear, hear!

This note underlines the dramatic consequences of such measures for refugees and asylum seekers in need of protection.

Mr. Speaker, I do not think the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard), the distinguished and dedicated Member for Roberval, intended to tar with the same brush our friends in the Church and the con men and criminals we should banish from our shores. That is the main reason why Clause 9, especially, should be amended.
Mr. Speaker, 1 support the principle of having a system that is fair and just for everyone, and which gives all prospective Canadians, both refugees and immigrants, the same opportunities. However, we must not act with undue haste. Some major changes must be made, and we will have to take another look at this Bill and do some fine tuning to prevent abuse. Believe me, we are all human and we all make mistakes. We will not all be sitting in this House ten years hence, and we must be sure this principles are upheld. Our successors may make mistakes as well, so we must provide for that eventuality.
If these amendments, which are necessary, are accepted, I will feel even better about the rest of the Bill. We can no longer let our system be abused by criminals who sell their services, when according to our concept of justice, everyone has the right to immigrate freely to our country, subject to certain conditions. In fact, we should put the perpetrators of this unjustified abuse, who use our laws to their own advantage, in prison for life.

Mr. Speaker, I want to thank the Hon. Member for La Prairie (Mr. Jourdenais) and I want to ask him whether he has any amendments to propose or suggest today. 1 would refer more particularly to Section 95.1 which affects those who aid or abet the coming into Canada of persons who are not in

possession of a valid and subsisting visa or passport and who belong to Canadian organizations such as churches and other types of organizations. How would he go about amending this Bill to reflect the principles he just described?

Mr. Speaker, to answer the Hon. Member's question, 1 mentioned in my speech just now that one clause, I believe it was Clause 9, should be amended specifically to protect church people in Canada. I said earlier in my speech that 1 had examined the Bill last night. I had to because I was very busy yesterday and I had not been able to look at the Bill.

I think Bill C-84 will match Bill C-55, and as far as I can see, the only clause we could amend is Clause 9. So I leave Clause 2 and if 1 remember correctly, you referred to Section 95.1

Mr. Speaker, 1 should like to commend the Hon. Member for La Prairie (Mr. Jourdenais), who is also the distinguished Chairman of the Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration. In addition to simply commending him, I should like to express a great deal of gratitude from our vantage point. The Hon. Member was not only correct and appropriate in the remarks he placed before the House of Commons this afternoon, but 1 think he also exhibited the courage and conviction to stay the course and to speak up for what is just and what is right despite being a member of the Government.
Those words will not be lost on this Chamber. Those words will not be lost on those Canadians who are looking very particularly at the House of Commons these days. They will understand that while Members on all sides clearly favour an end to abuse, there are also Members of Parliament, including Members on the government side, who are vigilant and wish to pass a proper and just piece of legislation.
Therefore, I think the Hon. Member has done this House and the interest of a progressive immigration policy a great service this afternoon, and I would appreciate his continued support.
In the dying minutes of the debate today, while the Hon. Member articulated some concerns about and amendments to Bill C-84, and in light of the fact that he said this Bill goes together with Bill C-55, perhaps he could share with the House any comments he may have in terms of amending Bill C-55, so that we have a package which is truly reflective of the spirit of Canadians in the last 15 years to 20 years when it comes to dealing with refugees and immigrants?

In response, and to thank the Hon. Member for compliments which were not really necessary, I acted simply, first like a man, a human being. 1 followed the dictates of my conscience. With respect to amendments to Bill C-55, I have about a minute left so I will not have time to elaborate, my colleague would know that we have already debated a number of them. To satisfy your curiosity, there is one concerning the prescreening test. We will discuss it when Bill C-55 comes up for debate.

PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   ORGANIZED CRIME ESTABLISHMENT OF ROYAL COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for a few minutes I want to deal with organized crime and that part of Motion M-44 which proposes the establishment of a Royal Commission to investigate and make recommendations on legislation to enable the Government to identify and appropriate the proceeds of organized crime.
First of all, Mr. Speaker, I should like to commend the Hon. Member for Trinity (Miss Nicholson) for her interest in this matter. I am sure all my colleagues realize how important it is

August 13, 1987
Organized Crime
for society that our legislation provide for the confiscation of the proceeds of organized crime.
A number of criminal activities-illegal drug trafficking, to name one-are often organized and carried out much like major corporation business operations. Those activities generate tremendous profits that are then used to finance other criminal activities and to infiltrate legitimate businesses.
It is estimated that organized crime includes all types of criminal activities that come under the general heading of continuing agreements between people for gainful purposes. It is believed that one of the most effective ways of reducing that kind of crime is to eliminate the profit motive by getting at the gains produced by it.
Although organized crime can derive tremendous profits from illegal activities, Canadian law as it now stands has no provisions for freezing, seizing or confiscating monies gained from crime. In 1976, for the first time in Canada, legislative measures were passed to deal with the possession of illicit gains. Section 312 of the Criminal Code makes it an offence to have in one's possession property unlawfully obtained by whatever means.
Investigations and prosecution of offences under Section 312 unfortunately proved ineffective because investigation powers and procedures capable of identifying, freezing and seizing criminal proceeds are not adequately developed, either in law or in practice. For instance, money deposited into a bank account and real property cannot be seized.
In cases where gains from criminal transactions cannot be identified, there is often no way to prevent the divestiture of property before judicial proceedings are completed.
The confiscation of proceeds cannot be ordered under Section 312 where the prosecution of an offence under that section leads to a guilty verdict.
The efficacy of confiscation procedures depends on the possibility of seizing property to ensure that it can be preserved until proceedings are completed.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   ORGANIZED CRIME ESTABLISHMENT OF ROYAL COMMISSION

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   ORGANIZED CRIME ESTABLISHMENT OF ROYAL COMMISSION
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker, for allowing to reinstate a degree of silence in this dignified Chamber.
As I said, the efficacy of confiscation procedures depends on the possibility of seizing property so that it can be preserved until proceedings are completed. That kind of procedure already exists in civil law where there is a danger that the property in dispute disappear before the court makes a determination as to how it should be disposed of.
The system of search warrants under the Criminal Code provides for the seizure and retention of all things that can be classified as evidence of an offence, instruments used to commit an offence; or the subject of the offence itself.
Those provisions do not apply to the proceeds of criminal acts unless they are indeed property or monies derived from the committing of an offence.
When it is impossible to seize the holdings physically, for instance when the proceeds have been put into real estates, shares or maybe bank deposits, the provisions of the Criminal Code are not far-reaching enough to allow for the seizure and freezing of these proceeds and no provision of the current penal code can prevent the accused from disposing of them.
1 should like to remind my hon. colleagues that the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada (Mr. Hnatyshyn) recently introduced in the House a Bill to amend the Criminal Code, the Food and Drugs Act and the Narcotic Control Act to deal specifically with the proceeds of crime. Bill C-61 provides our courts with new powers to seize the proceeds of crime and the police with new judicially-controlled investigative powers allowing for the search of people and premises and the seizure of assets. Finally, the Bill would provide third parties having an interest on a seizable assets with protective and redress mechanisms.
The Bill will create new offences in order to fight against the laundering of the proceeds of organized crime, illegal drug trafficking as well as the possession of property obtained through drug offences. If the Bill is adopted, it will provide an efficient tool for the fight against organized crime.
I recognize that the motion moved by my colleague the Hon. Member for Trinity (Miss Nicholson) is well-founded, but in view of the Bill introduced recently by the Government to fight against organized crime and especially against the accumulated proceeds of crime, I must oppose motion M-44.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   ORGANIZED CRIME ESTABLISHMENT OF ROYAL COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to take part in the debate this afternoon on motion M-44, moved by the Hon. Member for Trinity (Miss Nicholson), and to speak to the amendment proposed by the Hon. Member for York Centre (Mr. Kaplan), that the Royal Commission report to the House within six months of its appointment.
Mr. Speaker, this motion deals with one of the important issues of the day. It is worded as follows:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the
advisability of appointing a Royal Commission to investigate organized crime
in Canada and to include in its report observations and recommendations on:
1.	the extent to which organized crime is present and active in Canada-
2.	the extent to which organized crime is connected to the institutions of
Canadian society;
3.	action taken by the governments of other countries to investigate and
curtail organized crime activity;
4.	legislation to enable the government to identify and appropriate the
proceeds of organized crime;
5.	effective and appropriate punishment-
6.	possible guidelines-
Mr. Speaker, we have had some very striking examples in this country of illegal activities, and we have been able to deal
August 13, 1987

with these in very effective ways. I am thinking of the tainted meat scandal in Quebec and the colourful saga of the Dubois clan. There was an inquiry which at the time made it possible to put a stop to these activities and at the same time inform the public of their existence.
I believe that in 1987, a similar approach, and 1 am thinking of a Royal Commission of Inquiry, might prove beneficial. I know opponents of this procedure argue that the cost is too high, the process takes too long, and so forth. The amendment proposed by the Hon. Member for York Centre (Mr. Kaplan) to have the report submitted within six months of the Royal Commission's appointment would seem to deal with these concerns, at least with the concerns raised at the time. As for the financial side of the matter, I would like to deal with this briefly later on in my speech.
Mr. Speaker, in June the House spent a lot of time debating capital punishment, and so far hardly anything has been done to reduce the crime rate. We were promised a number of measures and studies, but we have yet to see anything tangible from the Government or the Committee on Justice and Solicitor General. I know that the Hon. Member for Ottawa West (Mr. Daubney), for instance, who chairs the Committee on Justice, has proposed to review the whole prison system and the whole problem of criminality.
Mr. Speaker, this issue is important, and the Hon. Member for Trinity (Miss Nicholson) should be congratulated on her initiative, which could be more effective, progressive and useful in the long term in attacking organized crime than the Government initiative of launching a debate on capital punishment, which, as we all know, was resolved by the decision of the House not to reinstate capital punishment in Canada. However, we are still waiting for this Government to take some practical action to reduce the crime rate and provide a feeling of security for Canadians in their own country.
As for the monetary aspect, Mr. Speaker, the cost of criminal activities has been estimated at $2.2 billion in Ontario, and at $10 billion in Canada as a whole. This is to reply to the economic argument that a Royal Commission is costly. We have to realize that the hidden costs of criminality, since criminals operate out of the public eye, amount to $10 billion a year. I imagine that a Royal Commission could cost us a few million dollars and that such an investment would surely yield a lot in return.
What we have to ask, obviously, is this: Would the economic advantages of attacking this problem and preventing abuses not benefit all Canadians? The answer is obviously yes. Naturally, if we can stop the rise of crime by keeping Canadians better informed about criminal activities, we could save substantial amounts and put a stop to these criminal activities.
I have not heard as yet the exact figure of what a Royal Commission would cost. I do not know whether it is available but at any rate, I think that those costs can easily be determined on the basis of other Royal Commissions. But I suggest,
Organized Crime
Mr. Speaker, that ultimately, there will be spinoffs and we will save money.
The Canadian people and the general public often do in a naive way, if you want, things that they consider quite trivial and that take place every day. For instance, in a tavern, they will bet on a hockey or a football game without being concerned with the consequences, even though that is in fact illegal. Because you are dealing with people who make a buck through bets on football or baseball games, or any other sport event, and those dealings take place in taverns or elsewhere and are organized by groups of people who are benefiting from those investments, I think that Canadians should know that illicit groups grab an enormous amount of money, taking advantage, as 1 said earlier, of that laxity, that lack of interest that some people have occasionally for common practices, bets in this case, and other events as trivial as a horse race or a baseball game. They think as many other people that they do not harm anybody, when they make a $2 bet on a horse or a football game. But in fact, Mr. Speaker, those two dollars are unlawfully laundered by illegal agencies and groups to their profit. This is how some unlawfully earned amounts of money are gradually embezzeled and used for illegal activities. Those funds will then be invested in other illegal activities which will bring about more money for those involved. That is why in Canada, every year, organized crime rakes in some $10 billion from unlawful activities. Being outside traditional economic systems, all the money does not benefit Canadian society very much. Indeed, it contributes to social degradation. Criminal activities generate human misery and, if I may say so, are the greatest misery inflation factors in Canada. The rich do not play those games and bet those two dollars, Mr. Speaker. More often than not, those with low or average income are attracted by such games, fall victims to and enrich profiteers.
For those reasons, Mr. Speaker, and I could cite many more but 1 think my time is almost up, 1 believe the motion brought forward by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Trinity (Miss Nicholson), is highly justified and timely. That is why 1 will vote for it, and I urge my colleagues in the House, regardless of their political affiliation, to do likewise.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, let me congratulate the Hon. Member for Trinity (Miss Nicholson) once again for her initiative, and I hope the Government will act on it in the near future.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise to speak to the amendment put to the motion of the Hon. Member for Trinity (Miss Nicholson). In doing so, I would like to commend her for bringing the issue of organized crime to the attention of the House. I fear, however, that the proposed Royal Commission to investigate organized crime might have an effect opposite to the one

August 13, 1987
Organized Crime
presumably desired by the Hon. Member who put the motion forward.
Some Canadians, perhaps influenced by the American media, have vastly inflated views and ideas of the extent of organized crime in Canada and of the extent of organized crime involvement in Canadian social, economic and political institutions. I certainly do not want to minimize the threat posed by organized crime in Canada, particularly in relation to drug trafficking, and indeed I cannot help but feel that in this area and some other areas of criminal activity, the matter of capital punishment ought not to be forgotten.
I note that the previous speaker made reference to what he termed the futility of such a debate. I certainly take issue with that statement and suggest that ultimately, society will revisit that area in relation to this very topic which is under discussion today. In any event, 1 am confident that the combined law-enforcement efforts of all Governments in Canada are becoming increasingly effective in controlling organized crime.
As well, I think it should be noted that there is no evidence of widespread organized criminal involvement in Canadian institutions. In my view, therefore, there is little benefit to be derived from establishing a royal commission to delve into these matters.
Again, contrary to the views of the previous speaker, the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier), I frankly fail to appreciate the spin-off dollar value about which he spoke relating to the establishment of a royal commission. Obviously, royal commissions are extremely expensive, and because the rules of evidence at such commissions are less rigorous than those in courts of law, the evidence adduced before such commissions cannot be used in court proceedings. Therefore, such proceedings would at best be of little value to law enforcement.
Moreover, 1 think it is possible that a royal commission could unnecessarily alarm Canadians by creating the impression that organized crime was not being adequately addressed by Canadian authorities and by the courts. In addition, one cannot help but be concerned that a royal commission could tend to deflect both attention and resources from ongoing intelligence and enforcement efforts and possibly retard the investigation and prosecution of these cases.
Just as important, the proposed royal commission might constrain ongoing federal, national, and international initiatives aimed at organized crime control. As I noted earlier, the federal, provincial and municipal Governments are already deeply involved in and heavily committed to controlling organized crime. National intelligence systems are in place and are being upgraded regularly. Police forces are combining their knowledge, experience and investigative skills in joint forces operations targeting major organized crime figures.
Major institutions, such as the Canadian banking community, are examining ways and means of minimizing the extent to which they can be used to launder money. Both federal and provincial government Departments are increasingly exploring the extent to which statutes other than the Criminal Code can be applied to the prevention or control of organized crime. Police training, both provincially and nationally, is being upgraded to ensure that officers have the knowledge and skills necessary to detect organized crime and to gather evidence required for the successful prosecution of major cases. These efforts are not widely appreciated and reported on in the Canadian media. In Canada we tend to proceed more quietly and with less fanfare than in the U.S.
In my view, the approach of Canadian law enforcement authorities to organized crime has been and is very effective. It focuses efforts and resources and reflects excellent cooperation between all jurisdictions in the prevention, detection, investigation and prosecution of organized crime figures. It is particularly concerned with the rights of persons who become innocent and unwitting participants in organized crime.
Law enforcement policy and activities operate to preserve the confidence of Canadians in the integrity of social, political and economic institutions as the major influences constraining the corruption that organized crime attempts to promote. Key to this is the integrity of Canada's police, courts and other law enforcement institutions as our front line defence against organized crime.
It has been stated that the criminal underworld in a given society is a direct reflection of the integrity and morality of the institutions of government and business. We must sustain policy and programs to ensure that Canada will never become a country in which the underworld can take root. This demands continued vigilance by governments and law enforcement authorities.
1 believe this Government recognized the Hon. Member's legitimate concern respecting organized crime. Canada continues to act in concert with the provinces to enhance enforcement efforts. A royal commission would add little to the mechanisms already in place or under development to deal with organized crime. Rather, this House should support and encourage the federal and provincial Governments in their law enforcement activities, including the expeditious handling of legislation designed to make the law more effective in dealing with organized crime.
While I am confident that the motion put forward by the Hon. Member for Trinity reflects serious concern over the extent of organized crime in Canadian society and the availability of measures to facilitate law enforcement efforts, I would like to assure her that members of the Canadian police community, and other dedicated criminal justice professionals, are acting competently in their response to the problem. They have the confidence of this Government and merit the support of all Members of this House, and Canadians generally. It is for those reasons, I believe, it would not be in the best interests
August 13, 1987

of Canadians and our efforts against organized crime to establish at great expense a royal commission which 1 believe would be of little use in attacking the problems and perils posed by organized crime to Canadian society.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am disappointed in the speech given by the Hon. Member speaking on behalf of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnatyshyn). We have heard the speech before and it did not address the important points brought forward in this debate. There is a sense of complacency, a feeling that everything that needs to be done is being done. I think that assertion has to be challenged on two grounds.
First, this is a legislative Chamber. We pass laws here. That is the prerogative and responsibility of this House, not of the police or the administrative arm of justice, but of legislators. It is clear that legislative change is required. The President's commission in the U.S. came forward with recommendations requiring major statutory change. Why would we abdicate our responsibilities when there is a clear need in that country to make changes? The Hon. Member seems to be assuming that everything that can be done, except in the area of reform legislation, is being done. I for one do not believe that we should have others take on our responsibilities. That is why I believe the proposal of the Hon. Member for Trinity (Miss Nicholson), as amended, is a proper response to the problem by a Member of the national legislative Chamber of this country.
My second ground is that one has to accept almost as a matter of faith that the problem is being handled. Yet what evidence is offered to support that claim? I heard nothing that would give one any sense of confidence that the worldwide problem of the laundering of drug money has somehow bypassed Canada. Yet that assertion has been made. One of the real values of a royal commission would be to tell us what is going on. 1 think it is particularly appropriate because of the changes instituted in other countries to deal with this problem. If they tighten their control, that will put pressure on the Canadian financial system if we have not made similar reforms. That kind of dirty money will find an outlet. If other countries apply new laws, then it is almost automatic that organized crime will try to find other countries to access. If we have turned a blind eye to the problem, it follows that we would become a target for that kind of penetration by organized crime in its efforts to find a safe haven for its immense financial resources.
I have another comment to make. 1 do so with some reticence but it has to be said. The Government's defence for not supporting this resolution is that it will cost too much. 1 read somewhere in the last couple of weeks that the legal fees the Government is paying for the defence of one of its former Ministers in front of a royal commission is now close to $1 million. The defence fund for Mr. Stevens was originally $200,000 and has now gone up substantially, to say nothing of the cost of the commission itself which I think has come close
Organized Crime
to $3 million. That was to investigate the alleged wrongdoings of one Minister of the Government. The Government is now claiming that it does not want to spend any money to look at the widespread problem of organized crime which affects a wide variety of activities for reasons of economy. I do not think that is a fair and proper balance of responsibilities. 1 am not necessarily condemning the actions of the Government with respect to the royal commission for Mr. Stevens and his actions.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   ORGANIZED CRIME ESTABLISHMENT OF ROYAL COMMISSION
speechtext:
1 am sorry, the Member for York Peel (Mr. Stevens). However, I am pointing out that the Government was prepared to do that but seems to be saying that we cannot afford that with regard to organized crime and its financial implications in Canada.
1 also do not agree with the argument that money spent on a royal commission would be taken away from law enforcement. It may well be that a royal commission, finding efficacious ways of dealing with the problem, could save a lot of money in law enforcement by learning where and how to implement effective measures. Rather than sailing blindly into this problem, we would know where to go.
I believe that the amendment which was introduced by the Whip of our Party is a real effort to ensure that there are limitations. The Hon. Member for Trinity is not prescribing a long-term pension plan for a royal commission. This is something which would be quick and to the point, would address the problems, and would pass the results back to the Government.
I wonder why there is this reluctance, this hesitancy to come to grips with the issue. Is it because it would expose things which the Government does not want exposed? I raise this not in an accusatory way but in a questioning way. It may be that there is some anxiety that a royal commission would reveal that we are not taking the proper measures to meet the problem and that a careful examination of the problem would reveal real weaknesses.
This is a Private Member's Motion with no partisanship attached to it. subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   ORGANIZED CRIME ESTABLISHMENT OF ROYAL COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 rise with very serious thoughts tonight in the House of Commons. Having been elected only in September, 1984, 1 take very seriously the remarks of my more experienced colleague, the Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy). 1 would like to congratulate my hon. colleague, the Member for Trinity (Miss Nicholson), on the motion she has presented. It is very important for us. I come from Quebec and perhaps I should speak in French.

Sometimes I feel 1 ought to speak in French. At the same time, Mr. Speaker, I would like all Canadian men and women to understand what such a measure means to us. So 1 will speak in English from time to time, and perhaps I will say a few words in French as well. But French-speaking men and women of Canada must know how important Bill C-61 is to us.

Organized crime is usually defined as the activities of a group of persons who seek to operate outside the control of the Canadian people and their governments. It can involve hundreds of criminals working within structures as complex as those of any large corporation, subject to laws which may be more rigidly enforced than those of legitimate governments. Its actions are not those of legitimate governments, but of conspiracies.
The core of organized crime activity is the supplying of illegal goods and services-gambling, loan-sharking, narcotics and other forms of vice-to countless numbers of citizen customers. Organized crime is also extensively and deeply involved in legitimate business. This is the danger. Here it applies illegitimate methods-monopolization, terrorism, extortion and tax evasion-to drive out or control lawful ownership and leadership and to exact illegal profits from the public. To carry on its many activities secure from governmental interference organized crime corrupts public officials.
Organized crime wants money and power. It is different from law-abiding organizations and individuals with those
same objectives in that the ethical and moral standards the criminals adhere to, the laws and regulations they obey, and the procedures they use are private and secret. They devise them themselves, change them when they see fit, and administer them summarily and invisibly.
Organized crime affects the lives of thousands of Canadians, but because it desperately preserves its invisibility many- perhaps most-Canadians are not aware of how they are affected or even that they are affected at all. The price of a loaf of bread may go up by 1 cent as the result of an organized crime conspiracy, but a consumer has no way of knowing why he is paying more. We cannot allow this to happen, Mr. Speaker.
It is organized crime's accumulation of money, not the individual transactions by which the money is accumulated, that has a great and threatening impact on Canadian society. Organized crime in Canada exists by virtue of the power it purchases with its money. The millions of dollars it can invest in narcotics or use for lay-off money give it power over the lives of thousands of people and over the quality of life in the legitimate economic system that presently exists in Canada.
The millions of dollars it can spend on corrupting public officials may give it power to maim or murder people inside or outside the organization with impunity. It will give it power to extort money from businessmen and to conduct business in many fields without regard to administrative regulations, to avoid payment of income tax.
The purpose of organized crime is not competition with visible, legal government but the nullification of it. When organized crime places an official in public office it nullifies law enforcement.
I am very serious about supporting the motion that has been brought forward by the Hon. Member for Trinity. As everyone in the House is aware, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnaty-shyn) tabled a Bill to deal with the problem of proceeds of crime. Bill C-61 proposes a number of amendments to the Criminal Code, the Food and Drugs Act, and the Narcotic Control Act, and addresses the problem of illegally obtained proceeds and assets by providing law enforcement agencies with the necessary powers to investigate, freeze and seize the proceeds of certain crimes and by providing the courts with the powers to confiscate the proceeds of these crimes.
I am sympathetic with the motion that has been brought forward by my hon. colleague, the Member for Trinity.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to stress again that it is not very often that we have the chance, the opportunity, to change and improve our laws.
Mr. Speaker, I believe, as the Hon. Member for Bonaventure-Iles-de-la-Madeleine, that it is important as Quebecers or as Canadians, that we recognize that it is our security
August 13. 1987

system and our body of laws which provide the means to fight the lawlessness we have in Canada, Mr. Speaker, and that the Government is here to guarantee our security and to protect Canadian men and women.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to address the House tonight and speak about drug trafficking. As the father of two young children, 1 can tell you, as most fathers and mothers across the country, that the drug problem is one of the worst problems that exist in the world today. To solve that problem in Canada and around the world, it is necessary that Canada co-operate with other countries to guarantee a better control at the international level.
Mr. Speaker, the motion before the House today highlights drug trafficking and its connection with organized crime. I would like to talk about the various measures taken by this Government.
The previous Solicitor General led, in 1985, the Canadian delegation to the seventh United Nations conference on the prevention of crime and the treatment of offenders, held in Milan. Hon. Members and Canadians will be glad to know that Canada played a leadership role in the drafting of measures to fight international drug trafficking. Besides supporting United Nations initiatives, in particular the new convention on illicit drug traffic, we are co-operating with members of the Economic Summit in the fight against drug abuse.
On April 25, 1986, Canada ratified, along with France, the United States and Italy an agreement on drug control. That agreement is the result of efforts made since 1970 by the four-power Conference including representatives from the Police nationale frangaise, the U.S. Bureau of Narcotics and Dangerous Drugs and Canada's RCMP. On March 4, 1986, Canada fully endorsed along with Italy the five-year agreement to prevent and eliminate the traffic in narcotics and dangerous drugs. Mr. Speaker, I think Hon. Members will be glad to hear that Canada will host here in Ottawa the coming four-power Conference next month.
I referred earlier to the development of a draft United Nations Convention on the illicit traffic in drugs. Canada cosponsored, on the occasion of the 39th Session of the United Nations Commission on narcotic drugs held in February, 1985, a resolution on the starting up of the development of a draft convention against the illicit traffic in narcotics and psychotropic substances. That new convention is viewed as a necessary and effective tool for the implementation of the measures against drug trafficking. A Canadian delegation including representatives from the secretariat of the Department of the Solicitor General and the RCMP attended in February 1986 an extraordinary session of the United Nations Narcotics Commission, where significant progress were made as to the identification of matters to be included in the draft convention.
Organized Crime
With the exception of certain matters concerning the control of ships and extradition, Canada generally supports the proposed provisions.
Canada views as a top priority the inclusion in the draft convention of a provision to allow each member State to trace, freeze and confiscate profits derived from drug trafficking. Most importantly, it will enact for its part domestic legislative measures making it easier to seize and confiscate those profits, especially those derived from trafficking in illicit drugs.
Another important proposed provision would be an essential tool against the manufacturing of forbidden drugs. It deals with the international control of the major precursors used in the manufacturing of forbidden drugs, for the purpose for instance of extracting heroine from opium and cocaine from coca.
Another still, dealing with controlled deliveries, that is the transportation of forbidden drugs under specified, known and police-approved conditions, is aimed primarily at extending the offence so as to allow the arrest and conviction of the major actors rather than simply seizing the drugs and arresting middlemen.
Controlled deliveries are an effective technique which, where successful, enables to identify the major conspirators and instigators and to go right up to the top of an international connection.
As far as mutual judiciary assistance is concerned, significant progress has been made in the area of international exchange of information aimed at fighting the illicit drug trade. Efforts from now on will be aimed at transmitting evidence and information that can lead to the seizure of profits derived from drug trafficking. Unlawfully acquired property to all practical purposes remains out of reach, by reason of conflicting national and international legal systems. The United Nations Narcotics Division decided to look at measures that could go against banking security rules that encourage the apparently legitimate accumulation of those illicit proceeds in countries recognized as tax havens. Meanwhile, Canada has ratified a treaty of mutual judiciary assistance it had with the United States and is currently negotiating similar agreements with Switzerland, the Bahamas and other Commonwealth countries.
The proposed convention deals with illegal drug trafficking by means of commercial carriers.
In most cases, air carriers and shipping companies are not held responsible for the illegal drugs hidden in luggage or on passengers, but they are held responsible when clearly their employees or crews are directly involved or facilitate the illegal activities through loopholes in their security procedures.
Another provision deals with cross-border co-operation.
Canada recognizes that co-operation between the various intelligence services within the international community is of vital importance and should be intensified in the future,

August 13, 1987
Message from the Senate
especially in the area of drug trafficking and the investment of its proceeds in apparently legitimate commercial enterprises. For the Government, encouraging co-operation between producing, transiting and consuming countries is therefore a priority issue.
The United Nations International Conference bn the Fight Against Drug Abuse and Drug Trafficking will be held next June in Vienna. Hon. Members are certainly aware that Mr. Tamar Oppenheimer, the Conference's Secretary General, is a Canadian who once headed the United Nations Drug Division. Moreover, Canada will be represented at the conference by a Minister, demonstrating the importance the Government attaches to it. Various problems will be dealt with during this multidisciplinary meeting, including the reduction of the demand, the development of alternative crops, the use of drugs for medical purposes, the seizure of drug-related proceeds, the treatment and rehabilitation of drug addicts, and the increase of law enforcement resources.
Also, Mr. Speaker, I cannot overlook the efforts made by the RCMP and the other provincial and municipal police forces.
Indeed, each year at the Canadian Police College the RCMP offer training to police officers from every corner of the world and they send experts to various countries, those of the Commonwealth included, to teach the skills required to fight against the different types of crimes we are talking about. People responsible for enforcing law in Canada, especially RCMP officers, work in close co-operation with their counterparts in other democratic western nations to fight against every kind of crime, particularly organized crime which knows no boundaries. This fight requires special skills and costs a lot of money, and this creates difficulties in times of financial restraints.
Mr. Speaker, given everything that is being done now I doubt whether a Royal Commission on organized crime would serve a useful purpose.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 rise today to pursue a question that I asked some time ago with respect to logging on Lyell Island.
What 1 am doing today is not pursuing the question, because the question that I asked at that time has been overtaken by events. Since I asked the question, there has been an agreement to have a national park in South Moresby. That is something a great many Canadians take a lot of satisfaction from. I thought it would be useful to take this opportunity to congratulate all those who were involved in arriving at that agreement. I wish to cite a number of people who I know were instrumental in making that agreement possible.
Perhaps I should begin with the Haida people themselves who, through their own spiritual and historical attachment to South Moresby, were one of the great sources of strength to those people who worked for so many years to have an agreement to create a national park in South Moresby.
One also needs to cite the great host of people who worked in a voluntary manner to advocate the creation of a park. There are too many of those people to begin to name them. 1 will not attempt to name them, because 1 would be bound to leave someone out.
One also has to cite people in this Chamber who were instrumental in bringing that agreement to fruition. 1 congratulate the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) for his involvement in bringing that agreement to fruition. I congratulate the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) for his involvement at the last minute, which one has to assume was instrumental in some way in making an agreement possible.
1 congratulate the Premier of British Columbia, Mr. Vander Zalm, for having been converted to the cause of having a national park in South Moresby, and resisting the temptation to settle for a provincial park only in that area.
1 congratulate the House for the part that it played in creating the appropriate political context for the people to act in who were pushing for a national park. I am thinking of the
Adjournment debate
day when we made procedural history in the House. We had a motion before us moved by the Hon. Member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton), who as a Member of Parliament for that area has been involved in the struggle to get a national park at South Moresby for many, many years. I am thinking of the day when we agreed somewhat early on in the day that the rriotion by the Hon. Member for Skeena would be deemed to have been passed and that we could then debate the motion. That unanimous expression of the House of Commons that day created a political context, not only for those outside the House, but also for Mr. Speaker himself to lend his good offices to contributing in whatever way he could to the creation of a national park at South Moresby.
Because the House of Commons had spoken unanimously, he was free to be an advocate of something which by that time had transcended partisan politics. A great many people contributed in many ways, and I think it is useful to put this on record.
Many other things need to happen. We go from this victory for a very special part of creation to other battles which have to be won. One is reminded of the continuing controversy over the Stein Valley, over the Stikine River, and over the Khut-zeymateen, an area which is special in respect of grizzly bears. Many issues yet remain to be solved. There will be lots of disagreement and debate in years to come about these matters.
However, I think it is appropriate to comment upon it when there is unanimous agreement in the House of Commons, when that unanimous agreement is followed by an agreement between the federal Government and a provincial Government-in this case, the Government of British Columbia-and when so many people have managed to put the best interests of the future above everything else and arrive at agreement.

subtopic: THE CONSTITUTION-PROMOTION OF FRENCH AND ENGLISH LINGUISTIC DUALITY-POSITION OF GOVERNMENT AND PROVINCES-INCLUSION OF SPECIAL PROVISIONS IN CONSTITUTION-PRIME MINISTER'S POSITION

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: THE CONSTITUTION-PROMOTION OF FRENCH AND ENGLISH LINGUISTIC DUALITY-POSITION OF GOVERNMENT AND PROVINCES-INCLUSION OF SPECIAL PROVISIONS IN CONSTITUTION-PRIME MINISTER'S POSITION
speechtext:
Last June 4, Mr. Speaker, I asked the Government a question concerning the provisions of the Meech-Langevin Accord, the 1987 Constitutional Accord, as it relates to linguistic duality.
Mr. Speaker, we know that section 2.(1 )(a) of the Accord signed by the ten provincial premiers and the Prime Minister of Canada, acknowledges the obligation of the Parliament of Canada and the provincial legislatures, and I am quoting word for word, to preserve the fundamental characteristic of Canada referred to in paragraph (l)(a).
Mr. Speaker, this section recognizes the existence of Frenchspeaking Canadians, centred in Quebec but also present elsewhere in Canada, and the existence of English-speaking Canadians, concentrated outside Quebec but also present in Quebec.
That is a basic point. For the first time in the history of Canada such recognition is given supreme status by being included in the Constitution. This is a major step for our country.
Better still, the signatories to the Accord went further by making it constitutionally mandatory for the Parliament of Canada and all provincial legislatures to preserve this fundamental characteristic.
This is a first step. But if they recognize the importance of our language duality by enshrining the principle in the Constitution, why was there not a will to allow it to develop by charging the provinces and the Canadian government with the additional obligation to protect and promote that basic feature? Why have we stopped half-way through that process? That was the heart of my question, the reason why I rose.
Since the agreement was signed, we heard many experts comment on the 1987 Constitutional Agreement. Most of them recognized that a strictly political problem prevented the addition of the obligation to promote language duality in addition to protecting it. Senator Murray, responsible for the matter and Minister in this government, recognized before the Committee that we tried but could go no further. This is too bad. It is too bad for the official language minority groups throughout Canada, either francophones outside Quebec or anglophones in Quebec, because the commitment is to maintain the status quo. Looking at statistics, the assimilation rate of the Canadian francophonie outside Quebec is rising constantly. On the other hand, the birth rate is very low, which means that if the French culture is not promoted outside Quebec, it may well disappear within a matter of years.
Mr. Speaker, the protection of minorities has been a commitment of the Canadian government for years. During the 1987 constitutional negotiations, the Canadian government bowed to provinces for political gains. It did not have the political courage to take on the obligation to promote language duality. We can understand and perhaps even explain that it could not convince the provinces to do that promotion. But that it does not take upon itself, as the Canadian government, not only the obligation to protect but especially the obligation to promote it, I find this, Mr. Speaker, a serious flaw in that constitutional agreement. The minorities, and I know what I am talking about, are disappointed. They were expecting more than that from the federal Government. In answers to questions here in the House and elsewhere the Government told us several times that it would promote linguistic duality through the Official Languages Act which, as you know, was tabled in the House last June.
August 13, 1987

Mr. Speaker, I say: Very well, so much the better! But I would remind Hon. Members that a statute is not the same thing as a constitution. It is very different. A constitutional obligation cannot be changed overnight. Near unanimity would be required to do so now. A statute can be changed, amended, repealed, indeed this is what we do here every day. 1 am afraid that it was a mistake not to have entrenched the obligation not only to preserve and protect, but also to promote linguistic duality, and this is why I wanted to know whether the Government intends to amend the Meech-Langevin proposal and to insert, at least at the federal level, the obligation to promote this duality.
Mr. Speaker, there is no need to recall in this House the examples we have had in past months and years of certain Federal agencies, such as the RCMP, which has often shown reluctance and even indifference about complying with the Official Languages Act even though it is a statute of Parliament. I believe that this obligation could be made much stronger by entrenching it in the Constitution instead.
I would ask the Parliamentary Secretary to explain to me whether the government might have changed its views and whether our large Canadian family, both French- and Englishspeaking, can expect to learn some time from now that the government will change its plans and propose an amendment to the Constitutional Agreement that does not obligate the provinces to anything, please note this, but that makes it an obligation for the Canadian government itself not only to protect but to promote. As suggested by the FFHQ, the Federation des francophones hors Quebec, we could add a provision allowing provinces to concur in the promotion when they so wish, each province individually. We could have a provision today saying that, the government binds itself to promotion, and provinces would do so in the form of provincial resolutions passed in the province's legislature, under which they could bind themselves to not only protect but promote.
Mr. Speaker, I ask the Parliamentary Secretary to transmit to his government the comments I just made and perhaps even to give us an assurance that he will himself defend, as I do, the idea of trying to convince the provinces and the Canadian government to accept to promote language duality, which is essential to us as a people so that we can survive here as full-fledged citizens wherever we live in this country.
