speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with interest to the comments made by the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier) who has in the past devoted much of his energies and, in fact, still does, to defending the French fact, for which he is to be commended. In fact, all Conservative Members from Quebec follow his example.
Today, he raised a question regarding the wording of subsection 2(2) of the Constitution Amendment, 1987 which
Adjournment debate
refers to the role of all legislatures in this country, including Parliament and the Quebec Legislature, to preserve Canadian Linguistic duality. This duality is described in subsection 2(1 )(a) of the amendment.
The Hon. Member has asked about the federal Government's role in promoting Canada's linguistic duality in light of the proposed subsection 2(2) of the Constitution Amendment, 1987. I can assure the Hon. Member that Parliament's role is as strong as ever and the Official Languages Bill, Bill C-72, recently introduced by the government, in June if I am not mistaken, is a perfect example of how Parliament can promote Canada's linguistic duality. Such measures can only find additional suport in the proposed new constitutional recognition of Canada's linguistic duality.
The Special Joint Committee on the Constitutional Accord is of course examining all the clauses of the proposed Constitution Amendment, 1987 in detail.
One of its great underlying features is the co-operative approach to federalism and this government is confident that such an approach is in the best interests of all Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, as you probably know, Japan sends its nuclear reactor waste by sea to Europe for reprocessing to recover plutonium which Japan would like to have back for use as a fuel in a new model nuclear reactor. In 1984, one shipment of plutonium was sent by sea from Europe to Japan without mishap. In January of this year, Japan and the U.S. finished five years of negotiations on a draft agreement to transfer up to 226 kilograms of plutonium, which can be used for making nuclear weapons, from Europe to Japan twice a month for the next 30 years. The current plan is to transport the plutonium in jumbo jets from Europe, over northern Canada, to Anchorage, Alaska, for refuelling and then on to Japan.
According to Thomas Homer-Dixon and Carolyn Lee, Canadian Ph.D. candidates at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Canada was advised but not consulted during these negotiations. The agreement is to be ratified by both countries next month and if Canada openly declares now that it will not allow these shipments, the political difficulties in the context of Canada-U.S. relations would be much less than they would be if Canada raised them when the agreement is delivered to the U.S. Congress for ratification. Then the difficulties will be very great. Therefore, the window of opportunity is open now.
The total amount to be carried over Canada is equal to about half the plutonium in the U.S. nuclear arsenal. It is to be

August 13, 1987
Adjournment debate
shipped as fine powder particles less than one-tenth of a millimetre in size. It does not dissolve in water, stick to soil, and cannot be absorbed by plants. According to Professor Rathjens at MIT, if such a powder is ejected into the atmosphere, as it could be in a large fire resulting from an airplane crash, "much of it could remain airborne for many days and, depending on particle size and meteorological conditions, could travel hundreds or even thousands of miles".
The radioactivity of any plutonium powder released in a crash would increase for several decades as a portion of it decays into a more dangerous isotope. Plutonium has a half life of hundreds to thousands of years depending on the isotope. Although plutonium is relatively harmless if touched or eaten, studies show that inhaling even a minute speck can cause cancer.
Canada has absolutely nothing to gain by allowing two jumbo jets full of plutonium to fly over the Canadian Arctic every month for the next 30 years. On the contrary, we have everything to lose. Even one crash out of the over 700 flights anticipated could kill people as well as caribou, polar bears, and other Arctic wildlife through the slow death of cancer as a result of inhalation of the toxic plutonium dust. Even residents of Yellowknife or cities further south, perhaps including Edmonton, could conceivably be threatened depending on wind and weather conditions, location of the crash site, and the extent of destruction to the casks carrying the plutonium. These risks are avoidable if we say no now.
In a letter to the editor of The Globe and Mail on July 31, 1987, Nobel Prize winner John Polanyi points out that we are dealing with "a total amount of plutonium equal to about half of that in the entire U.S. nuclear arsenal, with all the risks of diversion to military use that this implies. If such traffic proves to be expensive and cumbersome, that is all to the good". He recommended that if this material is to be shipped, it must be by sea under satellite surveillance and escorted by a convoy.
Therefore, my questions to the Parliamentary Secretary are these. Is the Government aware that the time to say no is right now, because the window of opportunity is expiring soon, and that after the agreement is ratified in mid-September the opportunity will be lost?
Second, has Canada already given permission for these flights? That was not at all clear from the answers of the Parliamentary Secretary given two days ago. Third, can the Government, the Minister, and the Parliamentary Secretary assure Canadians that the Government will notify Japan and the United States that Canada will now allow the overflights of plutonium? If it has already notified these two countries, we will be glad to hear about that right now.

speakeroldname: Mr. Gordon Towers (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State for Science and Technology):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the matter of the suggested overflights of Canadian territory by aircraft carrying some form of plutonium, I would like to make perfectly clear the position of the Government. First, I would point out that there has been no ratification of any agreement and there have been no decisions made at this time on routing of the material.
I would also reiterate, as mentioned by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) in March of this year, that the movement of all dangerous goods by air is subject to both international convention and domestic legislation. In the international arena, Canada is a signatory nation of the International Civil Aviation Organization, and as such Canada has a number of options available.
First, we can request that pre-notification be given and that approval be received prior to any overflight being taken. In this case we would insist that the most stringent requirements for safe packaging be met and that all safety and inspection requirements be met as well.
Our second option is to deny any overflight by filing a state variance with the International Civil Aviation Organization based on Canada's concern with any inadequate safety measures of such flights.
In the matter of Canada's input with respect to the U.S.-Japan negotiations, Canada made representations to the United States Government in May and August of 1986 and again at a very high level in April of this year to express our concerns in this matter.
In summary, the Government is monitoring this matter very closely. The permission of the Canadian Government would be required on a case-by-case basis before any such overflight could take place and no such overflights would be carried out without expressed Canadian approval. Canadian safety standards are among the highest in the world and any proposal would be fully scrutinized to ensure that these high standards are fully complied with, particularly in the area of safe packaging.
Finally, let me assure the Hon. Member that any decision taken by the Government would make the safety of Canada and Canadians the most important consideration.
